'''Sir Christopher Martin Dobson''' (8 October 1949 – 8 September 2019) was a British [[chemist]], who was the [[John Humphrey Plummer Professors|John Humphrey Plummer Professor]] of [[Chemical biology|Chemical]] and [[Structural Biology]] in the [[Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge|Department of Chemistry]] at the [[University of Cambridge]], and Master of [[St John's College, Cambridge]].<ref name=cv/>

==Early life and education==
Dobson was born on 8 October 1949 in [[Rinteln]], [[Germany]], where his father, Arthur Dobson was commissioned as an officer.<ref name=Who>{{Who's Who |author=Anon| title=DOBSON, Sir Christopher (Martin) | id = U13819 | year = 2014 |doi=10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.U13819| edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]}}</ref><ref name=":3" /> Both Arthur Dobson and Christopher Dobson's mother, Mabel Dobson (née Pollard), were originally from [[Bradford]] in [[Yorkshire]] and had left school at age 14.<ref name=":3" /> Dobson had two older siblings, Graham and Gillian.<ref name=":3" /> Due to his father's postings, Dobson also lived in [[Lagos]], [[Nigeria]].<ref name=":3" />

Christopher Dobson was educated at [[Hereford Cathedral Junior School]], and then [[Abingdon School]] from 1960 until 1967.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.abingdon.org.uk/uploads/school/files/abingdonian/1968_January_V014_N004.pdf#page=58|title=Chemistry Prizes|publisher=The Abingdonian}}</ref> He completed a [[Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge, and Dublin)|Master of Arts]] and [[Doctor of Philosophy]]<ref name="dobsondphil">{{cite thesis |degree=DPhil |first=Christopher Martin|last=Dobson |title=The conformation of lysozyme in solution |publisher=University of Oxford |date=1975|oclc=500426925 |url=https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:3590b04b-6127-462c-ace2-1e13cf93d15f|website=ora.ox.ac.uk|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.453735}}|author-link=Chris Dobson}} {{free access}}</ref> at the [[University of Oxford]], where he was a student of [[Keble College, Oxford]] and [[Merton College, Oxford]].<ref name=":3" />

==Research and career==
Dobson's research largely focused on [[protein folding]] and [[protein misfolding]], and its association with medical disorders particularly [[Alzheimer's disease]] and [[Parkinson's disease]].<ref name=Who/> By applying chemical and biophysical techniques, Dobson investigated links between protein structure, function, and disease.<ref name="Robinson">{{cite journal |last1=Robinson |first1=Carol V. |title=Christopher Dobson, 1949–2019: Mentor, Friend, Scientist Extraordinaire |journal=Annual Review of Biochemistry |date=20 June 2020 |volume=89 |issue=1 |pages=1–19 |doi=10.1146/annurev-biochem-011520-105226 |pmid=32343910 |s2cid=216647586 |language=en |issn=0066-4154|doi-access=free }}</ref>

He is well known for his serendipitous discovery that ordinary proteins can misfold and aggregate to form [[amyloid]] structures.<ref name=":3">{{Cite news|url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/healthcare/article/professor-sir-chris-dobson-obituary-z6s3t7jzq|title=Professor Sir Chris Dobson obituary|date=12 September 2019|work=[[The Times]]|access-date=13 September 2019|language=en|issn=0140-0460}}</ref>

{{Quote|text="A postdoc who left his sample of an unfolded protein in an NMR [nuclear magnetic resonance] spectrometer over a long weekend discovered, on his return, that it had turned into a gel. We were curious about this phenomenon and found that the NMR tube was full of amyloid fibrils that we then thought were associated only with diseases".|sign=Christopher M. Dobson|source=<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/healthcare/article/professor-sir-chris-dobson-obituary-z6s3t7jzq|title=Professor Sir Chris Dobson obituary|newspaper=[[The Times]]|date=12 September 2019}}</ref>}}

Dobson authored and co-authored over 800 papers and review articles,<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cambridgeindependent.co.uk/news/professor-sir-christopher-dobson-master-of-st-john-s-college-cambridge-dies-at-69-9082339/|title=Professor Sir Christopher Dobson, master of St John's College, Cambridge, dies at 69|date=9 September 2019|work=Cambridge Independent|language=en|access-date=9 September 2019}}</ref> including 38 in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'', ''[[Science (magazine)|Science]]'' and [[Cell (journal)|Cell]], which have been cited over 100,000 times.<ref name="scopus">{{Scopus|id=36042495400}}</ref> {{As of|2019}} his [[H-index]] is 153.<ref name="scopus"/>

Dobson held [[research fellows]]hips at [[Merton College, Oxford]] and then [[Linacre College, Oxford]] before working at [[Harvard University]]. He returned to Oxford in 1980 as a [[Oxbridge Fellow|Fellow]] of [[Lady Margaret Hall, Oxford]] and as a University [[Lecturer]] in Chemistry, later receiving promotions to [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]], then [[Professor]] of Chemistry in 1996.<ref name=Who/><ref name=":3" />

Dobson moved to the [[University of Cambridge]] in 2001 as the [[John Humphrey Plummer Professors|John Humphrey Plummer Professor]] of Chemical and Structural Biology. In 2007, he became the Master of [[St John's College, Cambridge]], a post which he held until his death in September 2019.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=https://www.joh.cam.ac.uk/tributes-paid-master-st-johns-college-who-has-died-age-69|title=Tributes paid to Master of St John's College who has died age 69|website=St John's College Cambridge|access-date=9 September 2019}}</ref>

In 2012, Dobson founded the Cambridge Centre for Misfolding Diseases,<ref name=":3" /> which is currently based in the Chemistry of Health building at the Department of Chemistry at the University of Cambridge.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cam.ac.uk/news/new-research-facility-for-neurodegenerative-disorders-opened-in-cambridge|title=New research facility for neurodegenerative disorders opened in Cambridge|date=21 September 2018|website=University of Cambridge|language=en|access-date=9 September 2019}}</ref>

In 2016, Chris Dobson co-founded Wren Therapeutics, a biotechnology start-up company whose mission is to find new therapeutics for Alzheimer's disease.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cambridgeindependent.co.uk/news/knighthood-for-prof-christopher-dobson-master-of-st-john-s-college-in-recognition-of-ground-breaking-alzheimer-s-research-9051085/|title=Knighthood for Prof Christopher Dobson, master of St John's College, in recognition of ground-breaking Alzheimer's research|date=8 June 2018|work=Cambridge Independent|language=en|access-date=9 September 2019}}</ref><ref name="Robinson"/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://endpts.com/cambridge-spinout-grabs-23m-round-to-launch-a-new-campaign-to-tackle-protein-misfolding/|title=Cambridge spinout grabs $23M round to launch a new campaign to tackle protein misfolding|website=Endpoints News|language=en|access-date=9 September 2019}}</ref>

===Awards and honours===
Dobson was [[knight bachelor|knighted]] in the [[2018 Birthday Honours|2018 Queen's Birthday Honours]] for his contributions to science and higher education.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.lmh.ox.ac.uk/news/knighthood-eminent-scientist-sir-christopher-dobson|title=Knighthood for eminent scientist Sir Christopher Dobson|website=Lady Margaret Hall|language=en|access-date=9 September 2019}}</ref> In 2009, Dobson was awarded the [[Royal Medal]] by the Royal Society "for his outstanding contributions to the understanding of the mechanisms of protein folding and mis-folding, and the implications for disease", and in 2014 he received both the Heineken Prize for Biochemistry and Biophysics and the [[Feltrinelli Prize|Feltrinelli International Prize]] for Medicine. Dobson was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 1996.<ref name=frs>{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/christopher-dobson-11340/|author=Anon|year=1996|title=Sir Christopher Dobson FMedSci FRS|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|location=London|website=royalsociety.org}} One or more of the preceding sentences incorporates text from the royalsociety.org website where: {{quote|"All text published under the heading 'Biography' on Fellow profile pages is available under [[Creative Commons license|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]].” --{{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161111170346/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/|title=Royal Society Terms, conditions and policies|date=11 November 2016}}}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Robinson FRS |first1=Carol V. |last2=Robinson |first2=Colin G. |date=2024 |title=Christopher Martin Dobson. 8 October 1949—8 September 2019 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=77|pages=129–143 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2024.0021 |doi-access=free }}</ref> His nomination reads: {{quote|Dobson is distinguished for his studies, principally using [[Nuclear magnetic resonance|NMR methods]], of the structures and dynamics of proteins in solution. Such studies include those on [[lysozyme]], with which he demonstrated many methodological advances, [[Interleukin 4|interleukin-4]], with which he established for the first time the topology of the important family of [[Haematopoiesis|haemopoietic]] helical [[cytokine]]s, and [[urokinase]]-type [[plasminogen activator]], with which he elucidated the dynamic characteristics of multidomain [[Fibrinolysis|fibrinolytic proteins]], Dobson is a pioneer in the application of NMR methods to the problem of protein folding, which is now the major theme of his work. His studies on lysozyme are resulting in one of the most detailed descriptions of a folding pathway for a protein. Dobson has explored the properties and reactions of molecules in solids by means of NMR spectroscopy, including [[protein]]s, [[Organometallic chemistry|organometallic compounds]], [[inorganic]] [[Paramagnetism|paramagnets]] and the silicaceous components of hydraulic materials. Notable here are analyses of the nature and origin of dynamic properties in molecular solids, and their relationship to structure and reactivity.<ref name=royal>{{cite web |url=https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=(RefNo==%27EC%2F1996%2F06%27) |title=EC/1996/06: Dobson, Christopher Martin |publisher=The Royal Society |archive-date=5 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170305002203/https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=(RefNo==%27EC%2F1996%2F06%27) |location=London |url-status=dead |df=dmy-all |access-date=30 September 2014 }}</ref>}}

=== Mentorship ===
Dobson mentored and supervised many notable [[PhD student]]s and [[Postdoctoral researcher|post-doctoral researchers]], many of whom became renowned experts in their own field. These include:

*[[Carol V. Robinson]] at the [[University of Oxford]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rsc.org/news-events/articles/2019/sep/chris-dobson-tribute/|title=Paying tribute to Chris Dobson|website=www.rsc.org|language=en-GB|access-date=16 September 2019}}</ref>
*[[Sheena Radford|Sheena E. Radford]] at the [[University of Leeds]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/sheena-radford-12133/|title=Membership to Royal Society|language=en-GB|access-date=27 September 2019}}</ref>
*[[Cait MacPhee]] at the [[University of Edinburgh]]<ref>{{cite tweet|author=Cait MacPhee|author-link=Cait MacPhee|user=sciorama|number=1172416493998366722|date=13 September 2019|title=Chris Dobson was a vocal and practical advocate of women in science before it was cool. The number of women he employed or appointed in Oxford led to us being called "Dobettes" (yes, we knew what you called us, you pricks).|language=en||access-date=27 September 2019}}</ref>
*[[Clare Grey]] at the [[University of Cambridge]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/clare-grey-11541/|title=Membership to Royal Society of Chemistry|language=en-GB|access-date=6 October 2019}}</ref>
*[[Brenda Schulman|Brenda A. Schulman]] at the [[Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry]] in [[Germany]]<ref>{{Cite web | url= https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/brenda-a-schulman-ikyy0i/| title=Membership to the National Academy of Sciences of the US}}</ref> 
*[[Michele Vendruscolo]] at the University of Cambridge<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Vendruscolo_Michele|title=Membership to Academia Europaea|language=en-GB|access-date=27 September 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www2.scopus.com/authid/detail.uri?authorId=7007094071|title=Citation metrics at Scopus|language=en-GB|access-date=27 September 2019}}</ref>
*[[Fabrizio Chiti]] at the [[University of Florence]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Chiti_Fabrizio|title=Membership to Academia Europaea|language=en-GB|access-date=6 October 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www2.scopus.com/authid/detail.uri?authorId=7004045049|title=Citation metrics at Scopus|language=en-GB|access-date=6 October 2019}}</ref>
*[[Andrew Baldwin (chemist)|Andrew Baldwin]] at the [[University of Oxford]]

== Personal life ==
Dobson met his wife, Dr Mary Dobson (née Schove) at [[Merton College, Oxford|Merton College]] at the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name=":3" /> They had two sons, Richard and William.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" />

He died on 8 September 2019, from cancer, at [[Royal Marsden Hospital]] in [[Sutton, London|Sutton]], near [[Surrey]].<ref name=":2"/>
